title: Nala and Damayanti
hook: in the forest, birds fly off with Nala's last cloth, and that night he cuts the one they share

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nala and Damayanti lost everything: one small lapse, a brother's dice, the children sent to safety, and a king walking out of his city in a single cloth. Your line was one small habit of care, done on purpose. What small habit did you do on purpose? Day seven hundred ninety-one.

Outside the city, Nala and Damayanti are hungry. Nobody will help them; Pushkara has made sure of that. Then Nala sees birds on the ground with wings that shine like gold, and he thinks: food. He throws his one cloth over them to catch them. And the birds rise into the air, carrying the cloth away with them. From the sky they speak. We are the dice, they tell him. We came to take even this. Now a king stands in the forest with nothing on at all.
screen: `GOLDEN BIRDS ON THE GROUND.` → `HE THROWS HIS LAST CLOTH.` → `"WE ARE THE DICE."`

segments.voice: So Damayanti shares hers. The two of them wrap themselves in her single garment and keep walking. As they go, Nala keeps pointing out the roads. This one leads south. That one goes to Vidarbha, your father's country. He says it more than once. Damayanti hears what he isn't saying, and she answers it. Why are you showing me the roads? she asks. I won't leave you. If you want, we'll both go to my father's house, and he'll honor you. Nala says he won't go back to her family like this. They come to an empty rest house, and they lie down on the bare ground, and Damayanti, exhausted, falls asleep. Nala can't. Kali is still inside him, and his grief is pulling at him. He thinks: if I go, she'll go home to her people. If I stay, she'll suffer with me. He finds a sword lying nearby. He cuts the cloth in half, as gently as he can, so she won't wake. Then he goes. Then he comes back and looks at her. Then he goes again. Then he comes back. The story lets him go back and forth, torn between love and Kali, until at last he leaves. Look at the week we've walked. It started with Arjuna on a mountain and in Indra's city, choosing restraint when he could have taken what was offered. It ends with Nala, not in his right mind, cutting a cloth in the dark. Both of these men are being tested. Tonight, one of them, with Kali still inside him, can't hold on. The sage keeps telling the story anyway, because it isn't over.
screen: `ONE CLOTH FOR TWO.` · `"WHY SHOW ME THE ROADS?"` · `THE SWORD AND THE CLOTH.` · then, large: `HE GOES, AND COMES BACK, AND GOES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone who has stayed with you when it would have been easier to go. You don't have to name the hard time. Just see their face. Breathe in, and let yourself remember that they stayed. Breathe out, and send them a quiet thank you, wherever they are. If a time comes to mind when you left, or someone left you, let it be there too, without judging it. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer. If not, simply stay with the memory of someone who stayed. The bell holds the time.
Vastra, the one cloth they shared. Carried off by birds at first, then this single garment, until a husband cuts it in the dark and leaves, and comes back, and leaves.
Your line: notice who stays beside you. Today, notice who stays beside you, and let them know you've noticed. Day seven hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: In the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata, the sage Brihadashva tells Yudhishthira how Nala left Damayanti sleeping in the forest; in this scene the couple are parted.

pairs: cuts the shared cloth in half

myth: they said they were the dice, come to take even his cloth.
Damayanti asked Nala to send her home
she asked why he kept showing her the roads and said she would not leave him.
Nala went back and forth before he left
the story has him leave and return more than once before he finally goes.

fork.setup: you're Damayanti, walking in the forest with Nala. he keeps pointing out the road to your father's country. what do you do?
options: ask him why he's showing you the roads, and say you won't leave him.
go on alone, ahead of him.
fork.reveal: she refuses to leave and offers to take him to her father's house, but that night, while she sleeps, he cuts the cloth and goes.

original.note: Sanskrit vastra: cloth, garment, like the one Nala and Damayanti share and he cuts in two.

trapdoor: what you thought: Nala abandoned his wife because he stopped loving her.
what it means: in the story, Kali is still inside him, and he leaves thinking she'll go home to safety.
what a scholar hears: the narration has him leave and return again and again, so the scene reads as a struggle, not a cold choice.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Nalopakhyana: the birds take Nala's cloth; the shared garment; the roads to Vidarbha; Nala cuts the cloth and leaves Damayanti sleeping)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the birds' words (that they are the dice) and that Nala uses his own cloth to try to catch them.
Confirm the empty rest house (sabha) and that Nala finds a sword nearby.

Day 791 is a week end (days 785–791): the teach looks back to Arjuna's austerities and the Nala days. Phrasing 'one of them, tonight, fails' is an interpretive framing of the story; soften if a Keeper prefers.
The 'south' road detail is paraphrased from Nala pointing out roads; confirm or cut.
Editor: original changed from Damayanti (already used on day 788) to vastra, cloth.
Audit: softened the narrator's verdict on Nala ('one of them fails') to keep Kali's role, as the text does.
